The gap — a productised, mid-market-accessible advisory-plus-tooling offer — is real, but partly occupied at the top by Simon-Kucher.

moat.why: Weak. Methodology is copyable, advisory relationships are people-dependent, and the billing-infrastructure vendors that own the implementation relationship could add a services layer. A proprietary pricing-simulation tool and a credible operator brand (published benchmarks, named outcomes) are the only realistic moats.

margins.why: Mixed. Advisory revenue is capacity-capped by scarce senior pricing talent; a software/tooling layer scales at high margin. Blended margin depends on how much value is pushed into the tool versus billed as bodies — an advisory-heavy mix keeps it moderate.

founderFit.why: The best fit of the team's recent ideas: management consulting plus finance/investment is squarely the skill set for pricing strategy and ARR-impact modelling, and the offer is services-led rather than needing a product-engineering team. The gap is domain-specific credibility — SaaS pricing is a specialist field with entrenched experts, and the team would be selling to software CFOs without an obvious track record in it.

risk.why: Moderate. Capital-at-risk is low (a services business) and the timing is excellent — repricing is a 2026 CFO emergency. Against that: advisory doesn't scale, 'migrate our pricing' can be a one-time project rather than recurring revenue, incumbents (Simon-Kucher, the big consultancies) are the default choice, and the credibility barrier is real.

businessCase.summary: A productised 'repricing-in-a-box' — a repeatable methodology plus tooling (a pricing simulator, ARR-impact and cohort modelling, metering-readiness assessment) that helps seat-based SaaS companies move to usage, hybrid or outcome-based pricing without destroying existing revenue. The timing is unusually good: AI agents are compressing per-seat licences, seat-based pricing is falling fast as a primary model, and a February 2026 sell-off erased over US$1T of software value on exactly this fear — so repricing has become a live CFO priority. It fits the team's consulting/finance strengths better than any recent idea, but it's an advisory-led business (hard to scale, people-dependent), the credibility bar to sell SaaS CFOs is high, and Simon-Kucher already blends pricing advisory with its own software at the top of the market.
businessCase.customer: Seat-based B2B SaaS companies — especially mid-market firms below the big consultancies' focus — whose per-seat revenue is threatened by AI-driven seat compression and who need to migrate pricing without churning existing ARR. Sold to the CFO, CRO or head of monetisation.
businessCase.market: SaaS is ~US$316B and growing ~19% a year, and the pricing shift is real and current — seat-based pricing fell from 21% to 15% of B2B companies' primary model in a year, hybrid rose to 41%, and a Feb 2026 sell-off wiped out over US$1T on seat-compression fears. The reachable market for a boutique offer is far smaller (pricing software ~US$1.9B by 2030), but the pain is acute now.
businessCase.model: A blend of fixed-fee diagnostic engagements, a subscription to the pricing-simulation/ARR-monitoring tooling, and potentially a success fee tied to realised uplift. Pushing value into recurring tooling — repricing is continuous as AI features evolve — is what turns a one-off project into recurring revenue.
businessCase.goToMarket: Lead with credibility: published pricing benchmarks and thought leadership (the proven playbook for operator-brands in this niche), then convert inbound into fixed-fee diagnostics and land-and-expand into the tooling subscription. Target mid-market SaaS underserved by Simon-Kucher and the big consultancies.
businessCase.costs: Low — senior pricing talent and the build of a pricing-simulation/ARR-impact tool. The binding constraint is access to credible senior pricing expertise, not capital.
businessCase.risks: Advisory is capacity-capped and people-dependent; 'migrate our pricing' can be a one-time project rather than recurring revenue; the big consultancies (Simon-Kucher, McKinsey/Bain/Deloitte) are the board-level default and billing-infra vendors could add a services layer; and the credibility to sell CFOs a revenue-at-risk methodology is the hardest early barrier. The timing tailwind could also prove a crowded, hype-driven moment.
businessCase.nextSteps: 1) Establish credibility first — who on or around the team can credibly advise SaaS CFOs on pricing, and can we publish proprietary benchmark data to earn trust? 2) Decide the wedge: pure advisory, or advisory as the front end to recurring simulation/monitoring tooling (the more scalable path). 3) Interview 5-10 mid-market SaaS finance/product leaders on willingness to pay and buying process. 4) Prototype the pricing-simulator/ARR-impact tool. 5) Map the partnership option — feed clients into a billing-infra vendor's rails rather than compete with them.

clarifyingQuestions: Who brings credible SaaS-pricing expertise and references — the entry tax here is convincing software CFOs, not building the tool?
Is this pure advisory, or advisory as the wedge into recurring pricing-simulation/monitoring software (the only path that really scales)?
Partner with a billing-infrastructure vendor (Metronome/Orb/m3ter) as the delivery layer, or stay independent and compete with Simon-Kucher and the big consultancies?
